title: Svenska OS
tagline: My Swedish textbooks turned into a course I actually use: capture a word, let AI enrich it, practise the chapter, review it later.

hero.alt: The Svenska OS dashboard: a Swedish greeting, an A1 to A2 progress bar at 50 percent, and four ranked tasks for the day
hero.caption: The daily dashboard answers one question — what should I study today — and is a live projection over the data rather than a streak counter.

problem: I am learning Swedish from A1 towards B2 and I already had the curriculum: the Rivstart books and a Swedish–English dictionary. What I did not have was a way to work through them daily. Language apps do not follow my books, and a chatbot will happily talk to me in Swedish without ever telling me which chapter I am behind on.
So the books stay the source of truth. The app is the layer that turns them into something I open every morning.
data: The three Rivstart course books and the Hippocrene dictionary, modelled as books → chapters → grammar topics, plus the vocabulary I capture myself as I read.
The book PDFs never leave my machine. They are excluded from the repository, and in production the buttons that would open a page in the textbook disable themselves rather than break.
built: Three layers: the content layer that models the real course; a learning engine with vocabulary, generated exercises and spaced-repetition review; and an intelligence layer that enriches words and explains grammar.

The loop is deliberately short. Find a Swedish word, save it tagged with the chapter it came from, and the AI fills in the translation, whether it takes *en* or *ett*, its forms, examples and a usage note. Practise the chapter against exercises generated from its grammar and your own vocabulary. Review with flashcards. A daily dashboard answers one question — what should I study today — as a live projection over the data rather than a streak counter.
result: It is deployed on Vercel against a hosted Postgres database, and it runs without an API key at all: enrichment falls back to a manual stub, so the app is never blocked on configuration.
It is the tool I use for my own Swedish, which is the only test it was built to pass.
technical: The AI lives behind a service layer. Feature code never imports the Anthropic SDK — it calls `enrichWord()`. Output comes back through tool-use and is validated with Zod at the boundary, so there is no prose parsing to go wrong.

Two decisions were made to be reversed later. The scheduler sits behind a swappable interface — a transparent interval ladder today, FSRS when I want it — and a `User` row exists from day one even though the app is single-user, so adding authentication is a `where userId` change rather than a redesign.
SQLite locally, Postgres in production: enum-like fields are stored as strings and validated in the application layer, which makes the provider swap a config change.
